name: Erik Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential; you can say what you'd tell people and what you think privately. Walk me through a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 27, with a master's in software and a lead role at a tech company. I check the release pipeline, write fixes, and chase the odd bug that only shows up after a customer logs in; getting that bug to sit still is satisfying. The late releases wear me down, especially when my student loan payment is due the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the small assistant that drafts test cases is fine if someone still checks the result. We have a backlog of dull checks, and I don't mind clearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work is steady today, but my pay is low for someone who leads the release pipeline. My student debt takes a fixed bite, I have maybe two weeks of expenses saved, and there are few other tech firms nearby. That matters more than the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekly release routine and use the test assistant only on sample code, the way I sometimes do now. In December I'd put the overtime payment straight against my card balance; if there is no overtime, I can't invent savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little relieved about the job, still tight in the chest when I open the banking app. The flat doesn't get cheaper because AI failed to change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did the card balance come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card balance is from moving for this job and replacing my laptop, not holidays. I pay it down when there is extra pay, and I won't pretend a budget can squeeze water from stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your manager make of the small tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager likes the test assistant because it saves an hour here and there. I tell him the failures still need a human to reproduce them; last month it marked a broken login as passed.

say: I'd use the **test assistant** on sample code if a developer checks the result.
I'd point out that **broken logins** can still slip through automated tests.
think: My **student debt** and low lead pay leave about two weeks saved.
I have few **nearby tech firms** to turn to after even an ordinary job loss.
do: Keep the **weekly release routine** and review assistant output on sample code.
Pay down the **card balance** with December overtime if overtime arrives.
feel: **Relieved** about the job, but strained by existing bills.
S0.quote: The flat doesn't get cheaper because AI failed to change the world.
fieldNote: **Debt and low pay** keep his household anxious in the mildest picture.
He tests **AI output** pragmatically, yet remembers a false pass on a broken login.

steps.text: Keep weekly software releases and review sample test output
Pay down the moving and laptop card balance with December overtime if paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our team should try coding tools where they actually save time, with checks that everyone can see. If planning, coding, and customer answers shift to software, we can't pretend the old staffing plan still fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the release pipeline and write plenty of code myself. A smaller team could keep me for oversight at first, but once the tool does routine fixes, the company may decide it needs fewer developers, including a lead. I can't afford a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a four-week trial on old bug reports, record missed faults, and show the results to my manager. I'd also ask whether I can take on the security checks no one currently owns, and in the first year I'd save any pay from extra shifts rather than replace my laptop again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, with a bit of interest mixed in. I like a good tool; I don't like being measured only by how many tickets it closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your trial measure besides speed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tool once wrote a tidy fix that changed the wrong permission. I caught it in review, which is why the trial needs a count of bad fixes, not just a count of fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for the security work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't promise myself a security role until our manager budgets for it. If there is a paid opening, I'd take a short security course after work and ask the senior engineer to review my practice work.

say: I'd propose a **four-week trial** with visible checks and missed faults counted.
I'd ask for an **honest staffing plan** as coding and planning move to software.
think: I could lose my lead post when **routine fixes** shrink the team.
My two-week cushion would vanish during a long **income gap**.
do: Trial the coding tool on **old bug reports** for four weeks.
Ask about a **paid security opening** before taking a short course.
Save any **extra-shift pay** in the first year instead of buying a laptop.
feel: **Anxious** about staffing, yet interested in a useful tool.
S1.quote: I like a good tool; I don't like being measured only by how many tickets it closes.
fieldNote: **Measured faults** matter more to him than tool speed alone.
His security plan depends on a **paid opening** and review from a senior engineer before spending on a course.

steps.text: Run a four-week coding trial using old bug reports
Take a short security course if a paid opening appears
Save extra-shift pay instead of replacing the laptop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 would hit software code right away; the robots around 2031 are beside the point for our desks. I'd ask the company to publish what people will still be paid to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our code-writing posts to shrink sharply, and I might be one of the people let go. Two weeks of savings won't cover even a careful search, and my student loan keeps coming. This is the first picture where I might have to leave town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep writing and checking releases while asking my manager this month for a written redeployment plan, and I'd call the lender about hardship terms before missing a payment. If I lose the job in the first year after 2028, I'd take a paid maintenance technician opening at my uncle's workshop if one exists, then stay with my uncle for up to three months while I find my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I could work hard and still be looking at a rent notice with no software openings close by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the workshop job already available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle repairs commercial printers, and he has said I can stay for a short spell, not that he has a job waiting. I would ask about pay and the work before resigning from anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management for in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask for names and dates on the redeployment plan. A cheerful meeting about the future won't make next month's loan payment.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches coding before 2031 robots matter here.
I'd ask for **named paid roles** in a written redeployment plan.
think: I could lose my **coding job** quickly with only two weeks saved.
I might have to **move** because local openings are scarce and debt payments continue.
do: Keep **writing and checking releases** while requesting a written redeployment plan.
Call the **student lender** before any missed payment.
If dismissed, ask about **paid printer maintenance** and temporary lodging with my uncle.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible rent notice and little time.
S2.quote: A cheerful meeting about the future won't make next month's loan payment.
fieldNote: **2028 AGI** threatens his coding income directly; 2031 robots do not delay that.
The **uncle's workshop** offers neither a promised job nor indefinite housing, so he checks both.

steps.text: Keep writing and checking releases while asking for a redeployment plan
Apply for a paid printer maintenance opening if dismissed
Stay with his uncle for up to three months if dismissed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the 2031 thinking system gives us years to test new roles before code writing is cheap everywhere. The hands-on robots follow around 2034, so I wouldn't count printer repair as a permanent shelter without checking demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me clear debt if my pay holds, but the word if is doing a lot. I'd have a better shot at a security or repair role if I could show real work before the whole market shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a record of every security fault I find and ask for a paid move onto that work next review cycle. If the company agrees, I'd take an evening security course; in the first year after 2031, I'd apply for security posts only if the work still needs people and the pay covers my debt and rent. I'd check printer shops too, but I wouldn't move just for an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more able to breathe than in the two-year picture. A five-year plan can be revised when the pay numbers change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The security course costs about one month's rent. I'd ask the employer to pay, or wait until the card is cleared; I can't put another fee on it just to feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your uncle about repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my uncle that repair could be a backup, not a rescue promise. If robots reach shop floors around 2034, I'd want evidence that his customers still pay for human service.

say: I'd ask for a **paid security path** before 2031.
I'd say **2034 robots** make repair work uncertain too.
think: I could clear **debt** in five years if my wage holds.
I need proof of **real security work** more than a course alone.
do: Record **security faults** and ask for a paid transfer next review cycle.
Take an **evening security course** only after a paid transfer is agreed, if work funds it or my card clears.
After 2031, apply only to **security posts** whose pay covers rent and debt.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to revise a five-year plan.
S3.quote: The security course costs about one month's rent.
fieldNote: **Course cost** is concrete, so he will not finance it on an already strained card.
He separates **2031 code risk** from 2034 robots and checks whether repair remains viable.

steps.text: Log security faults and request a paid security transfer
Take evening security course after paid transfer agreed, if employer funds it or card cleared
Apply for security posts after 2031 only if pay covers debt and rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to build evidence, clear debts, and see which work customers still value. Coding is still exposed when thinking AI arrives in 2036; I don't get extra years merely because robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be 37 with a cushion and a security job, or 37 still living from pay to pay. I won't call ten years safety unless I actually use them. I would like to keep building software if someone still pays people to own the mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the card first, then save six months of expenses while keeping my release skills current. I'd take a funded security course if work offers one and collect examples of faults I fixed; in the first year after 2036, I'd compare paid security and release posts before moving. If neither pays enough, I'd ask the printer workshop about real vacancies, not assume family can carry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this month's rent, but almost hopeful. The deadline is distant enough to build options without gambling the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a six-month cushion realistic from here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months is ambitious from where I am. I'd start with one month and check each quarter whether my wage has kept up with rent and the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about a future human role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager who signs off when an automated release breaks a customer's account. If the answer is still a person, I want to know what that person is paid.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** still reaches coding before 2039 robots.
I'd ask who is **paid to own** failures in automated releases.
think: I need to **clear debt** and build savings before a decade feels useful.
I might find paid human release work, but I cannot count on **client demand**.
do: Clear the **card balance** before targeting six months of savings.
Take **funded security training** if my employer offers it.
Compare **paid posts** in release work and security in the first year after 2036.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent, yet hopeful that ten years could build options.
S4.quote: I could be 37 with a cushion and a security job, or 37 still living from pay to pay.
fieldNote: **Ten years** supports gradual debt reduction, though he doubts a six-month cushion is automatic.
His future choice rests on **actual wages** and who carries responsibility for automated releases.

steps.text: Clear the moving and laptop card balance before building six months savings
Take employer-funded security training if offered
Compare paid security and release jobs after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I'd need a written path to paid work, short-term relief on the loan if I was cut, and a real vacancy to apply for, not a promise that everyone will become a supervisor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the customer when the code is wrong. Someone still has to answer the phone and put the account right; I'd want that responsibility named before anyone calls a system ready.

headlineQuote: Someone still has to answer the phone and put the account right; I'd want that responsibility named before anyone calls a system ready.
portrait: At **27**, Erik leads software releases and fixes customer bugs at a tech company after earning a master's degree.
His **student loan**, moving costs and low lead pay leave roughly two weeks of expenses saved.
He sometimes tests **AI tools** on sample work, but checks faults and asks who owns failed releases.
Steady change threatens **staffing**; fast AGI could force a job search and temporary move to his uncle's home.
With more time, he would seek **paid security work**, clear debt and compare actual wages before changing jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his coding income before his small cushion supports a search.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid-work path**, temporary loan relief and real vacancies would help after a cut.
